item.title: ChristianMahnke.de: Tomy Puckman: Pac-Man before the Name Change
item.description:
Another handheld console, though not quite as old as the last one…

This is a very special find, because what would later become world-famous under the name Pac-Man is still called Puckman here.

The game was produced by the Japanese company Tomy, which was known for its electronic games in the 1980s and 1990s. It was originally released in Japan in 1981 (one year after the arcade version) and is believed to have been released in Germany in 1983.

You’re probably familiar with the rules of the game: You guide Puckman through a maze to eat the points while being chased by four ghosts. You can either dodge them or—if you have the right power-up—even eat them yourself (temporarily). The game ends when you’ve used up all your lives.

The game itself was also sold under the name “Munchman”.

The game can also be found in various collections:

  • At The Strong National Museum of Play
  • Electronic Plastic
  • Handheld Games Museum

A review of the console can also be found on YouTube:

ChristianMahnke.de: Brutalist Architecture in Bad Driburg
item.description:
Now the photos from my penultimate visit to a spa town are back from the lab…

Following my last brief travelogue about Bad Nenndorf, here are a few photos from Bad Driburg. Of course, the changed circumstances mentioned in the last post also apply in Bad Driburg, but here some of the effects can be observed more directly. One of the most striking is certainly this building, which is quite prominently visible from Brunnenstraße:

This is the former Hotel Neuhaus at Steinbergstieg 18, which closed in 2009. In 2018, an investor expressed interest, but so far, nothing has changed regarding its condition.

Another sign of times past is the condition of Café Heyse, which closed for good in 2022. On the first floor, an impressive collection of the now-disused seating can be seen.

The fact that Bad Driburg had actually anticipated growth in the late 1970s is evident in the development around “Am Hellweg”: a largely empty, parallel pedestrian zone that, with its combination of commercial spaces and residential units, looks like something straight out of a textbook on urban planning from that era.

All the photographs were taken with a Canon AE-1 using Agfa APX-100 film.

item.title: ChristianMahnke.de: AI for structural metadata
item.description:
The Kinderbücher (children’s books) now have structural metadata…

They can be found behind the “Contents” button and viewed in the viewer.

What’s “special” about them is that they’ve been created entirely with the help of an LLM.

My previous OCR experiments with AI haven’t always yielded the desired results, but that was mostly because I was expecting coordinates at the same time – something that general-purpose LLMs aren’t really capable of; all they do is make them up. However, for the simple mapping required in this case, their capabilities are more than sufficient: the model simply needs to recognise which text appears on which page. This yields the chapters, along with simple structures such as the book cover and spine. The latter (and a few others) were specified via the prompt.

And as the example [Father is at War (https://xn–kinderbcher-zhb.projektemacher.org/post/vater-ist-im-kriege/)] shows, even Fraktur script is no problem.

Incidentally, the book 1x1 des Tapezierens – Versuch’s mal selber! on Vorsatzpapier has also been processed, and it shows that even nested structures work. It demonstrates a different approach: in the case of this book, only the table of contents (and, initially, the pagination sequence) was recognised. This approach is quicker and more cost-effective because not every page had to be processed.

item.title: ChristianMahnke.de: IIIF 3D
item.description:
This blog has also featured 3D models for about 2.5 years. They can now also be viewed via IIIF (V4) in manifests.

IIIF Presentation V4?

IIIF (Presentation) V4 has been a long time in the making and has been undergoing the release candidate review process since April 2026. A key new feature is support for 3D data. The new container for this is Scene, alongside which (or rather, within which) Model is used. In addition to models, lights and cameras can also be placed within a scene. Models can be used in the glTF (or GLB as a binary format). Further information and examples can be found at the IIIF 3D Technical Specification Group, including sample manifests.

The manifests

The 3D models on this blog (for 3D models in the browser and UV photogrammetry) are now also available as IIIF manifests.

All pages with 3D content, their manifests and the respective link to the Kasane viewer:

Page Manifest Viewer
3D models in the browser manifest.json Kasane
UV photogrammetry manifest.json Kasane

Viewer

A manifest is only half the battle; you also need a viewer that can display the Scene class. Kasane (formerly “IIIF 3D Viewer”, University of Tokyo) is an open-source viewer (MIT) that displays 3D models, images, audio and video from IIIF manifests and can enhance them with annotations. The project has not yet been published on npm, but manifests can already be accessed via deep links:

https://kasane.ldas.jp/viewer?iiif-content=<URL of the manifest>

item.title: Blaufußtölpel: Catalina
item.description:
Da der Sommer vorbei ist, gibt es hier Bademode zu sehen, die ohnehin schon etwas länger aus der Mode ist.

Dieses Faltblatt ist eine deutsche Werbung für die amerikanische Firma Catalina Swimwear (engl.). Auffällig ist, das als Materialien Lastex (engl.) und Baumwolle angegeben werden. Das spricht dafür, dass dieses Faltblatt aus den frühen 50ern stammt, denn sonst gäbe es sicher auch Modelle aus Nylon.

Bei der Recherche zu diesem Beitrag ist mir übrigens aufgefallen, dass Bademode und Werbung aus den USA gesammelt werden.

item.title: ChristianMahnke.de: Art Deco architecture in Bad Nenndorf
item.description:
As you get older, you find yourself visiting places you wouldn’t even have thought of ten years ago. In recent years, these have increasingly been spa towns.

Health resorts hold a peculiar fascination for me. They are like time capsules where, for example, you can see independent shops from sectors that are now almost entirely dominated by chains in cities. At the same time, the effects of the dismantling of the welfare state are often evident. In the late 1990s, the number of preventive care and rehabilitation facilities peaked; since then, the number of clinics and beds has been declining (as shown in the graph). And even though the sector is in decline, spa operations have been and remain a source of income, just like tourism. As a result, spa towns usually have a stronger local economy than other towns of a comparable size. This leads to a healthier local retail sector and also to architecture that is more impressive than average.

This weekend we went to Bad Nenndorf for a family trip to the State Garden Show (German). Although that’s not what this is about, just to say:

  • The maze was a disappointment.
  • They could have fitted every drinks stall with a coffee machine.

On the way back to the station, this relief caught my eye:

It forms part of the entrance to the Wincklerbad (German) (in the Lower Saxony Monument Atlas (German)), built in 1930. Due to low occupancy rates in 2007, the former spa facility was sold and converted.

And I remembered that I had seen a few less conspicuous façade ornaments from this period (1920–1930) in the city. Back then, ornaments featuring geometric or at least abstract shapes and jagged edges were all the rage. They can be attributed to the Art Deco style of the 1920s. Bettina Vaupel published an overview article in Monumente Online in April 2012 (German).

As I was already on my way back, there are no photos of my own here, only views from Google Street View.

Hidden

Location: Rodenberger Allee 1,

This ornament is rather hidden and only visible from a side street. The arrangement and the surrounding marble wall with rounded edges are also very unusual. The arrangement is most likely not original. It is possible that the reliefs were removed prior to a refurbishment or renovation and arranged in this way so that they could continue to be displayed.

Transformed beyond recognition

Location: Buchenallee 13

Apart from the ornate entrance, this building, too, looks considerably newer, perhaps dating from the 1990s. If it was a conversion, then the alterations were far more extensive than in the previous example, as can be seen from the window lintels.

As both buildings are likely to have strayed considerably from their original form, they are probably not listed as Architectural monuments.

Another mystery

But then I saw this building.

Location: Parkhotel Deutsches Haus, Bahnhofstraße 22

And that’s when I asked myself: “Could it be that architectural style elements are simply being recycled in Bad Nenndorf?”

More

Hindenburgstraße begins across from the Parkhotel Deutsches Haus. The buildings at numbers 2 through 10 feature authentic Art Deco facade elements.

Epilog

There are numerous illustrated books and publications on the architecture of spas and health resorts, but for the 20th century (particularly the second half), there has been rather little so far…
